overview: Cheyenne history connects earlier communities around Minnesota with later Plains villages, mobile hunting groups and powerful alliances. The broad western polygon shown in 1492 should not be treated as a verified Cheyenne border for that year: the documented westward migrations came later. Northern Cheyenne and Southern Cheyenne communities continue today; the imported 1783 cutoff is not their ending.

periods.title: Earlier eastern homelands
periods.summary: The early western outline is misleading beside evidence for communities farther east. These are map years, not a founding date.

periods.title: Moving into the Plains
periods.summary: Different groups migrated west and adopted changing combinations of village farming and horse-based hunting.

sections.title: A history with farms as well as horses

items.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ historical account remembers Cheyenne cultivation of corn, beans and squash before the later hunting economy. Fields and settled homes therefore belong in this history too. The familiar image of a mounted buffalo hunter captures one important period, not every generation.

At Biesterfeldt in eastern North Dakota, archaeologist W. Raymond Wood described a fortified village of roughly sixty earth lodges, dated about 1750 to 1790. A larger lodge faced a central plaza. The Cheyenne identification is plausible but circumstantial, so the ruins cannot simply be labelled with certainty.

Biesterfeldt pottery resembles wares from Missouri River farming villages. This helps archaeologists compare how communities made and used everyday vessels, even where written records are sparse. Wood argued that migration happened in separate groups, with settled villages existing in more than one river region at once.

sections.title: A buffalo robe represented many days of work

items.text: In 1846 to 1847, traveller Lewis Garrard watched Cheyenne women stretch hides on the ground with wooden pegs and thin them with scraping tools. The National Park Service’s study reconstructs this work from his account. A robe ready to trade had already required substantial processing.

Softening continued over several days before smoking the hide. Finished robes entered a market for warm clothing and carriage coverings far beyond the Plains. The work of women in camp helped keep distant customers warm; the commercial story starts well before the trader counted the goods.

A Northern Cheyenne scraper attributed to Lame Deer combines elk bone, hide ties and metal. The object entered a museum loan in 1921, although its earlier history is unknown. Its mixed materials show practical toolmaking that incorporated metal into a shaped animal-bone handle.

A deer-bone cup-and-pin game was collected from Little White Man in Montana in 1924 or 1925. The museum records its pieces as strung together. This particular object preserves a trace of recreation alongside more frequently displayed weapons; its catalogue does not give enough information to recreate the rules.

The Cheyenne Dog Soldier Ledgerbook contains 106 coloured-pencil drawings by fourteen artists. The ruled pages of an ordinary account book became a place to record people, clothing, horses and events. Artists adapted a new material to established practices of representing personal and collective history.

The ledger’s scenes concern events between 1864 and 1869, and the book was recovered after the attack at Summit Springs. Cheyenne people and historians have identified particular artists and events through its detailed images. These are pictorial accounts, not sentences that can be translated word for word.

On 29 November 1864, United States volunteers attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village at Sand Creek, killing children and adults. Calling this a massacre matters: it was not simply a meeting of two armies. Remembering the victims remains part of Cheyenne public history.

Northern Cheyenne families resisted removal to Indian Territory and some fled north in 1878. After further suffering and conflict, families resettled in Montana, where a reservation was established in 1884. Their return explains why Northern and Southern Cheyenne histories need distinct geographical chapters.

The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ own webpage writes “Tsistsistas” and translates it as “Human Beings” or “The People.” This is an attested modern written self-name, using the spelling published by the community. It is separate from the pictorial storytelling of the nineteenth-century ledgerbook.

The same tribal language programme offers community and online classes, supports language learning in Head Start and child care, and pairs adults with experienced speakers in a Master Apprentice programme. Language learning therefore includes small children, working adults and elders, rather than ending when school finishes.

ending.text: The map stops in 1783, long before nineteenth-century massacres, warfare and forced reservation settlement. Cheyenne people continue in the Northern Cheyenne Tribe in Montana and in the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma, as well as elsewhere. These contemporary communities should not be collapsed into one vanished Plains state.
